Title: A Wider Pizza Slice Makes You Go Faster
Description: Toes out, heels in: the pizza slice shape is how you get moving from standing. What nobody explains is that the width of that slice is a throttle. A narrow V gives gentle, controlled propulsion. Open it wide and you accelerate harder than you meant to, which is how a first session ends up feeling out of control. If you pick up speed too fast, do not change the movement — close the angle. Inline technique, from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Illustration generated with AI.

Title: Take Shorter, Quicker Steps When You Start
Description: Beginners almost always slow their stepping right down, because slow feels careful and careful feels safe. It is the opposite. A slow step leaves you standing on one skate for a long time, and one skate is exactly where a beginner has no balance yet. Short, quick steps keep your weight moving between your feet instead of parking it on one of them. It feels less elegant and it is far more stable. Inline technique, from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Illustration generated with AI.

Title: Balance Starts Under Your Soles, Not in Your Head
Description: Before you fix anything else, learn to feel your own footprint: which part of each sole is taking your weight right now. The sole is a part of the body nobody thinks about, and it is where your balance is actually decided. Practise it on grass, on carpet, even in ordinary shoes — no rolling required. Skaters who build this awareness stop guessing about their position and start correcting it. Inline technique, from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Illustration generated with AI.

Title: Wobbly Ankles Are Almost Never Weak Ankles
Description: If your ankles roll inward, you have probably tightened everything and done ankle exercises, and nothing changed. It is not a strength problem — it is alignment. The ankle drops in and gives you a permanent inside edge. Three things cause it: loose straps, boots too wide for your foot, and not enough knee bend. Speed skaters have powerful legs from deep knee bend, not from isolating ankle muscles. Inline technique, from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Illustration generated with AI.

Title: New Gear Will Not Skate for You
Description: Thousands of videos about boots, frames and wheel sizes quietly teach one false idea: that different equipment produces overnight change. Here is the test. Does everyone running a rockered frame have beautiful flowing curves? Clearly not. A rockered frame helps you achieve those curves — it does not create them. Your gear should suit the skating you do, and that is all you can ask of it. Inline technique, from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Illustration generated with AI.

Title: You Would Never Skate Forwards Like That
Description: Watch people skating backwards and you see the same thing every time: both skates flat on the ground the whole way, wiggling side to side. Now picture doing that forwards, both feet glued down, shuffling along. You would call it hopeless, and so would everyone. Nobody notices it backwards because nobody sees themselves. Backwards uses the same principle as forwards: push with one skate, glide on the other. Inline technique, from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Illustration generated with AI.

Title: Backwards Skating Is Really a One-Leg Problem
Description: Most skaters stuck going backwards think they need more backwards practice. They do not. Both skates stay glued to the floor because they cannot carry their whole weight on the weaker leg while travelling backwards — so they never dare lift the other. The thing to train is not backwards skating at all. It is single-leg support on your weaker side, which you can build going forwards. Inline technique, from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Title: A Barrel Roll Is Three Moves You May Already Have
Description: The barrel roll looks like one continuous trick and it is not. It is an assembly of three separate things: a forwards-to-backwards transition, a backward crossover, and a backwards-to-forwards transition. If you can do those three on their own, you are not learning a new move — you are joining three moves you own. If one is missing, you now know which one to practise. Inline technique, from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Illustration generated with AI.

Title: The Hockey Stop Is Probably Not Your Next Stop
Description: The hockey stop, or parallel slide, is the one everybody wants and it sits at the top of the difficulty list for most skaters. That is not a reason to give up on it — it is a reason not to make it your current goal. The stop worth your next few months is the powerslide from a forwards entry: far more realistic, and the one experienced skaters reach for in traffic and on slopes. Inline technique, from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Illustration generated with AI.

Title: There Are Four Powerslides, Not One
Description: Skaters give up on the powerslide because they think there is one correct version and their body will not do it. There are four. Two ways of turning into it, two legs you can slide on — four combinations, and one will suit you far better than the others. Find your combination, perfect that one, then build the speed up very slowly. Skaters who own this stop say it changed how fast they are willing to go.
